blocks.tested_text:
Neuropsychological evaluations of people who have experienced an acquired brain injury (ABI) are often incomplete. This research addressed this by exploring whether the use of "clustering" would allow for a consistent representation of cognitive function despite two challenges: What method(s) would be used to replace missing information from the evaluation? How could the characteristics of cognitive ability be represented?

The historical component of the research included 17,406 assessments of 7,285 patients across six different areas tested using fourteen tests. Ten methods of imputation were used as part of the research. Using UMAP+HDBSCAN, a three band description of overall severity was generated based upon the entire set of data. Across imputations, the fixed-reference method resulted in a mean adjusted Rand index (ARI) of 0.710. While there seemed to be a number of small associations between the cluster groups and the clinical units, there was no clear added patient-grouped predictive value beyond broad diagnostic classifications. These findings did not establish distinct cognitive phenotypes.

In addition, the exploratory portion of the research was completed by taking the first eligible assessment for each individual patient. There were 5,828 discovery patients and 1,457 validation patients. Preprocessing was fitted within the discovery sample prior to conducting clustering within the original data space. In addition to clustering using the original data, the exploratory portion utilized several alternative methods including: Robust mixture models fit to the observed data; Twenty independently refit stochastic imputations; Fifty patient subsamples; Mixed-effects trajectory models.

Two-group k-means clustering was selected in each of the 20 imputation screens. The average pairwise validation ARI for these cluster analyses was 0.959. ARI for three-group k-means was slightly lower (0.935). Changing from robust to equal-domain scaling resulted in large changes in the three-group assignments (ARI = 0.243). Test availability differed across groups. In terms of fit with the observed data, robust t mixtures performed better and preferred an eight-component solution, the upper limit allowed during model selection. Among the 2,013 patients eligible for longitudinal assessment, multi-class trajectory models introduced groups below the specified 5% size threshold.

Therefore, we have shown there to be evidence supporting replicable grouping of cognitive test results based on certain assumptions regarding representation and imputation. However, it cannot be concluded that these groupings represent separate clinical phenotypes or could be used for treatment purposes. Additional independent measures of outcomes and additional samples from external cohorts will need to occur before clinical use. Acquired Brain Injuries (ABIs) consist of traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), stroke, encephalitis and hypoxic-ischemic injury. The clinical implications of ABIs are large. TBIs account for millions of emergency department visits/hospital admissions every year [Maas et al., 2017; Brazinova et al., 2021] ; ABI can also cause long-term disabilities for adults of working age, with physical, behavioral/emotional and cognitive changes [Corrigan et al., 2010]. The areas that are typically impacted by ABI include attention, memory, language and executive functioning but vary significantly from one patient to another.

The variation makes it difficult to develop individualized treatment/intervention plans based upon cognitive assessments of ABI patients. Post-ABI follow-up evaluations can identify patients who have sustained injuries of the same severity and yet demonstrate vastly different cognitive patterns and abilities. Commonly used criteria (diagnostic category or severity banding) grouping together different cognitive profiles will obscure clinically meaningful differences between individuals with identical diagnostic/severity categories [Saatman et al., 2008].

This research aims to investigate the above-stated concerns empirically. As opposed to applying previously established clinical taxonomic criteria to the dataset used for this research, I apply an unsupervised clustering method to group patients by their performances as measured on multiple neuropsychological tests, and then examine the extent to which the groups (subgroups) obtained from such application are clinically relevant. Another common obstacle to conducting analyses with clinically-derived data involves missing values. Clinicians often leave out components of neuropsychological testing batteries when administering them due to time limitations, patient fatigue, clinician judgment, or patient-related issues which may impede the completion of all test administrations. Non-random omissions of some test items are therefore anticipated.

Missing value imputations allow for retaining incomplete assessments; however, each procedure has its own assumptions about missing values. There is minimal documentation regarding how those assumptions affect subsequent cluster analysis, thus the relationship of those assumptions to cluster analysis is investigated directly within this dissertation.

The process of phenotyping represents the identification of cognitive subgroups through a data-driven process. The question remains unanswered as to whether these subgroups constitute qualitative differences in cognitive profiles or represent continuum levels of general severity.

The purpose of this study was to answer the following four research questions:

Research Question RQ1: Is it possible to isolate discrete cognitive phenotypes through the use of an unsupervised clustering method applied to the imputed dataset on participants with a history of an acquired brain injury?

Research Question RQ2: How much does the choice of an imputation methodology impact upon the identification of cognitive phenotypes?

Research Question RQ3: Are there associations between patient cluster assignment and clinical unit assignment? Such an association would suggest that cognitive tiers differ in their distribution among the populations served by different units.

Research Question RQ4: Can either (a) increased stability in grouping or (b) improved interpretation occur if the clustering utilizes composite scores representing domain areas as opposed to using individual tests in the clustering?

The objective ultimately is to create a reproducible phenotyping procedure based on routine clinical data collection. Missingness will be modeled as part of the rehabilitation process rather than treated as a nuisance only after data collection.

I test four hypotheses in this dissertation.

Hypothesis H1: My expectation using the UMAP/HDBSCAN pipeline is that there will be at least two cognitively stable clusters for most imputation methods. Also, I expect at most 30% of all data points to be labeled as noise, and the average silhouette score will be at least 0.40.

Hypothesis H2: I used the "fixed reference" from Chapter 3 to test if group assignments were consistent across different imputation methods. Specifically, I expected the median pairwise ARI between imputations to exceed 0.50. As stated previously, I would view this as evidence that the assignment is robust to these specific imputed data sets, but it would not rule out artifacts shared by the representation or establish clinical phenotypes.

Hypothesis H3: Chi-Square tests assessing association between cognition cluster membership and Clinical Unit population should show statistically significant results. I expect the value of Cramér's V to be greater than 0.10. These results would demonstrate differences among the populations served by clinical units.

Hypothesis H4: By aggregating domain specific features, I expect the same level of separation among groups, but lower levels of redundancy. Metrics that I will use to determine if this is accurate include silhouette values, Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), and Condition Number (CN).

An exploratory patient-level extension followed the historical H1-H4 analyses. It independently refits clustering across imputations and patient subsamples, compares feature scaling and incomplete-data mixture models, and models longitudinal cognitive scores. Methods and results are in Sections 3.8 and 4.12. It does not retrospectively redefine the original hypotheses.

blocks.section: Acquired Brain Injury and Cognitive Assessment
blocks.tested_text: Acquired brain injury (ABI) refers to brain damage sustained after birth that is not due to a congenital or degenerative condition [UK Department of Health and Social Care, 2022]. It includes traumatic and non-traumatic injuries such as traumatic brain injury (TBI), stroke, encephalitis and hypoxia/ischemia. Although there are many different etiologies of ABI, their commonality lies within their shared rehabilitative challenges and outcomes. Cognitive deficits post-injury will frequently influence long term functional status. One way that clinicians assess cognitive deficits that result from these types of injuries is through administering standard, normed neuropsychological tests. Most standard test batteries are designed to assess individuals' abilities across multiple domains of cognition. This includes assessing an individual's ability to visually/spatially process information, process language, engage in tasks requiring executive functions, learn and retain new information, and finally, how quickly an individual can process information. Each domain assessed has practical implications. Examples include, but are not limited to, attention deficit impeding an individual's participation in therapeutic interventions, memory impairments limiting an individual's ability to develop effective compensatory strategies for daily living activities, limitations in executive and language skills contributing to issues with planning, self-advocacy and communicating needs, and visuospatial impairments impacting an individual's ability to independently navigate their environment. Thus, a cognitive profile generated through comprehensive administration of neuropsychological testing can provide valuable information for planning rehabilitation programs, assist in establishing medicolegal issues related to the injury, and inform return-to-work decisions.

blocks.tested_text:
People who suffer from moderate to severe traumatic brain injuries (TBI) can have lasting cognitive problems, and there is no one way for people to recover from their injuries. Long-term studies have examined functioning for up to ten years after injury [Ponsford et al., 2014]. In their review, Rabinowitz and Levin [2014] describe that the cognitive outcome depends upon a number of factors related to the injury itself as well as the patient's history, including the patient's age at time of injury and pre-injury neuropsychiatric status. Injury severity alone therefore cannot fully describe an individual's cognitive profile.

Neuropsychologists will typically use modified versions of standard test batteries based upon such variables as: what specific questions were posed in the referral; the patient's tolerance for testing; and clinical judgment. Each of these decisions introduces additional variability/structured missingness into the resultant data sets. Therefore, multivariate analyses need to take this structured missingness into account rather than simply viewing the missing values as merely a minor methodological concern.

blocks.tested_text:
Although missing data occur frequently in clinical research [Gravesteijn et al., 2021], three mechanisms are distinguished [Rubin, 1976]: missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR) and missing not at random (MNAR). Missing completely at random (MCAR) indicates that missingness is unrelated to all values (both seen and unseen). Missing at random (MAR) implies that missingness may depend upon the observed values, but once those values are accounted for, then there will be no dependence on the missing values. Missing not at random (MNAR) suggests that missingness remains dependent upon the unseen values even when the observed values are considered.

Each type of missingness affects what statistical methodologies should be employed to produce reliable estimates. Under MCAR, listwise deletion is unbiased, but reduces the sample size and usually the efficiency of the study. When MAR exists, both multiple imputation and maximum likelihood estimation allow for valid inference under an appropriately constructed model. MNAR models require sensitivity analysis because observed data alone cannot establish assumptions about unobserved values [Rubin, 1987].

This understanding is especially important within clinical neuropsychology. Consider someone with severe attentional impairment who lacks the energy to complete an executive-function task, or a disoriented patient who is not given a memory test. In both examples, the missing value may be related to the value that would exist if the full test had been administered. Therefore, MAR is merely assumed as opposed to being definitively proven. MNAR patterns can coexist with missingness caused by assessment protocols. Although observed data alone cannot identify the missingness mechanism, auxiliary variables can make MAR more plausible by incorporating clinically relevant information [Little and Rubin, 2019].

Predictive mean matching selects observed donor values, keeping imputations within the observed range. This avoids impossible values, such as a negative score on a test with a floor. A limited donor pool can lead to repeated use of the same values.

MissForest utilizes iterative random forests for its missing value imputation algorithm [Stekhoven and Bühlmann, 2012]. For the first step, for every variable j, a forest f_j is created based on all instances of j where j is known. All other variables are treated as predictor variables. Next, a missing value is replaced by using the newly constructed forest f_j. The process repeats until changes are small.

Since MissForest does not assume parametric distributions, it allows the discovery of complex relationships between variables and can also be applied to either continuous or categorical variables. Generally, MissForest often performs well on benchmark datasets. A significant drawback of MissForest is that it can be quite time consuming and its computational efficiency decreases rapidly with increasing amounts of data or number of trees.

Clustering is used as a statistical technique in neuropsychological research. Clinical judgments about diagnosis or disability after stroke, traumatic brain injury (TBI), or in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) often rely on categorical assessments. Across many different types of clinical populations (e.g. TBI; MCI), cluster analysis has been used. Many of the resultant analyses have indicated that the statistically derived groups of performance within the realm of cognition do not consistently match the clinical diagnosis or severity category that are given to those same populations. Therefore, from an empirical perspective, it appears that when clinicians utilize classification systems to describe cognitive variability among individuals post-injury, they do not fully capture the full range of cognitive variability present.

A literature review of data-driven cognitive phenotyping after brain injury was conducted by [García-Rudolph et al., 2021]. Trends were consistent in their reviews. First, many of the studies found two to four statistically defined cognitive clusters. Second, many of the studies found clusters based upon whether certain cognitive domains were more functional than others relative to an individual's overall level of functioning. Third, when possible and relevant, researchers found that group membership was significantly related to clinically important outcomes (i.e. return to work).

blocks.tested_text:
Many aspects of research on data-driven cognitive phenotyping following brain injury are still underdeveloped. Many prior studies have been based on samples that ranged from approximately 100 to less than 200 subjects. The common practice among researchers was to exclude missing values by using complete cases. When missingness is MCAR (completely at random) this approach may be suitable for determining the characteristics of the remaining sample; however, when there is some degree of information within the missingness, then the use of complete cases can bias the resulting sample. Very few studies have investigated how sensitive clustering algorithms are to various parameter choices.

Therefore, this dissertation employed four distinct approaches to reduce the impact of these limitations. In Chapter 3 I used a much larger clinical database; compared ten imputation strategies to each other and to complete case analyses; examined sensitivity to hyperparameters and to several missingness thresholds; and tested HDBSCAN as an alternative method to k-means. Unlike k-means, HDBSCAN does not require the number of clusters k to be specified before application. Instead HDBSCAN identifies clusters where the density of data points exceeds certain threshold(s); data points which do not fit into a cluster are identified as "noise" or outliers.

The clustering process is composed of two key components: the UMAP for reducing the dimensionality of the input dataset and identifying clusters using HDBSCAN.

The first part (UMAP) applies a type of non-linear manifold learning. It seeks to reduce high-dimensional datasets to lower-dimensional representations while retaining as much of their original structure as possible. Because PCA and other forms of linear reductions cannot capture non-linear relationships present in the original data, UMAP can. As such, there are trade-offs involved with preserving the overall topological features of the data (i.e., globally) versus the local details, so we use three parameters to find a suitable balance between global and local structure:

* n_neighbors: This determines the number of neighboring points in the original data that should be used in the construction of each point's neighborhood graph. The larger this value is, the broader your view will be of the global properties of the data. Conversely, if you choose smaller values, you will have better insight into local relationships.

* min_dist: This governs how closely points can be placed together in the reduced space. If you increase this value, it results in spreading points farther apart from one another; conversely, setting it to a smaller value allows for denser grouping of related points.

* n_components: This is the target number of dimensions in the reduced space.

HDBSCAN represents data through a hierarchy of clusters at varying levels of density and identifies groupings that persist across that hierarchy. With respect to the recovery of variable-density and nested clusters, DBSCAN suffers in comparison because it uses a constant radius. HDBSCAN's explicit density hierarchy addresses this limitation. It selects stable clusters without requiring their number in advance and assigns the remaining observations to noise. Three key parameters govern its operation:

* min_samples - Density estimation parameter.

* min_cluster_size - Minimum size of a valid cluster.

* cluster_selection_epsilon - Distance threshold used to merge nearby clusters.

To connect observations, HDBSCAN uses mutual reachability (Equation 2.15), which adjusts distances to reflect local density. A minimum spanning tree over those distances provides the basis for the hierarchy. Successive levels form groups of observations, and cluster persistence is assessed through stability (Equation 2.16). For a given cluster C, λ_birth(C) is the density level at which C first appeared; λ_max(x,C) is the highest density level at which x belonged to C. Observations outside the selected persistent clusters are assigned to noise.

The ability to extract structure from high-dimensional datasets has led to applications of UMAP and HDBSCAN in computational biology and related fields.

HDBSCAN provides hierarchical clustering of the data at multiple densities and identifies the elements of the data that appear consistently throughout many of the different possible ways of grouping the data. In comparison, DBSCAN has difficulty recovering variable-density and nested clusters with a single fixed radius. HDBSCAN addresses these limitations by providing an explicit density hierarchy. It selects stable clusters without requiring a fixed number of clusters and labels other points as noise. There are three primary parameters to HDBSCAN.

* min_samples: This is the density estimation parameter.

* min_cluster_size: This is the minimum cluster size that will be considered valid.

* cluster_selection_epsilon: This is the distance threshold for merging nearby clusters.

In addition to adjusting the distance metric for each point so it is consistent with the density of that location, HDBSCAN uses mutual reachability, defined in Equation 2.15, to connect observations. A Minimum Spanning Tree constructed over the adjusted distances becomes the basis for a hierarchical representation of the data. Each observation is represented and then groups of observations are formed progressively. Next, the persistent clusters are determined based on how stable they are; i.e., based on Equation 2.16, where λ_birth(C) indicates the density level at which cluster C was first established, and λ_max(x,C) is the maximum density level at which x belonged to cluster C. Any remaining observations not assigned to one of these persistent clusters are labeled as noise.

Due to their ability to extract structured relationships from high dimensional datasets, UMAP and HDBSCAN have found application in areas including computational biology and related fields.

blocks.tested_text: Internal validation involves several aspects of cluster analysis. In this research we have used silhouette measures [Rousseeuw, 1987] to provide comparison of how well points in a cluster are cohesive (i.e., similar), with respect to how separated they are from points in their nearest neighbor cluster(s). A silhouette value will be a number in [-1,+1]. Silhouette scores greater than 0 indicate that a point is closer, on average, to other points assigned to the same cluster than to any other cluster. Scores close to 0 indicate little difference among those alternatives; while negative scores indicate that the point is actually closer to another cluster. These values do not determine whether an assignment is clinically correct. Each silhouette measure is calculated as per Equation 2.17, and is composed of two components: a(i); the mean distance between each point and every other point in the same cluster; and b(i); the mean distance from the point to every member of the nearest alternative cluster. The overall average silhouette for a set of clusters can be found by calculating the average of all s(i) values and will serve as our primary method of internally evaluating the quality of the clusters generated. Noise percentage is also reported. It is the proportion of observations left unassigned by density clustering and therefore describes its coverage.

Comparing cluster models for the same observations (e.g. cluster assignments generated using different imputation techniques), can be achieved by evaluating the degree of concordance among the resultant cluster models. An effective way to perform this evaluation is through the application of the adjusted Rand index (ARI) [Hubert and Arabie, 1985]. This metric evaluates the degree of concordance between the pair-wise cluster assignments to evaluate if the concordance exceeds chance.

To utilize the formula shown in Equation 2.18, we must first identify two clusterings of n objects denoted as U = {U_i} and V = {V_j}. We will also need to identify contingency counts denoted as n_ij = |U_i ∩ V_j|, where i and j index the clusters in U and V. The marginal totals denoted as a_i = ∑_j n_ij represent the number of elements in U_i. The marginal totals denoted as b_j = ∑_i n_ij represent the number of elements in V_j.

When ARI is maximally positive (+1) there exists a complete concordance between both cluster models. Conversely, ARI values which equal 0 indicate that the concordance observed between both cluster models equates to a chance baseline. Finally, negative values of ARI will indicate less than expected concordance between both cluster models [Robert et al., 2020].

In addition to the usage of ARI I also make use of normalized mutual information (NMI). NMI quantifies how much one cluster model provides information about another clustering, while providing normalization with respect to the entropy of each cluster model label.

The results of comparing the cluster assignment solutions through mutual information (i.e., I(U;V)) and Shannon entropy (i.e., H(·)) [Shannon, 1948] as expressed in Equation 2.19 can range from 1 when there is perfect agreement among cluster assignments to 0 when they are found to be statistically independent.

To measure the degree that clusters in one solution are either similar or dissimilar to those in another solution, I utilize the Jaccard Index. As indicated in Equation 2.20, where A and B represent the sets of observations that comprise the clusters being evaluated for similarity, the Jaccard Index represents the size of the intersection of the sets divided by the size of the union of the sets, with values in [0, 1]. Therefore, larger values of the index would indicate that the cluster memberships are more similar.

In addition to evaluating the similarity/dissimilarity between clusters across two solutions, I utilize clusterwise stability matching [Hennig, 2007], to evaluate whether cluster assignments remain stable after repeated sampling. In each of R resampling iterations, I pair an original cluster C_k with the resampled cluster having the greatest Jaccard overlap with it. I then average these maximum overlaps across the iterations. This average value is referred to as the "stability score" for C_k and is expressed as in Equation 2.21. A per-cluster score > 0.7 is used here as the stability criterion.

Taken together, NMI and ARI enable a quantitative comparison of similarities and differences between two cluster assignments. Although both metrics enable an evaluation of agreement between two cluster assignments they are metrics that measure agreement and should not be used as statistical tests of significance.

blocks.tested_text: The overall scores for the domains were determined by calculating an administration-frequency-weighted mean of the variables that represent the respective domain. Each variable j received a weight w_j = 1 - r_j, with r_j representing its missingness rate; weights were then normalized within each domain. Thus, variables that are measured more often will have a higher weight and therefore have a stronger impact when computing the domain score. In addition, the less frequent variables are reduced in their contribution to the domain score due to reliance on imputation of missing data. These weights do not measure psychometric reliability: they estimate neither internal consistency nor test-retest reliability or measurement error. Aggregating fourteen variables into six domain scores gives distance-based methods fewer dimensions to operate over. Clinicians who evaluate patient cognitive function based on a composite of multiple tests may find evaluating cognitive domains (e.g., attention, executive functions) easier to interpret than assessing individual test results. However, there is a trade-off in that two individuals receiving equivalent average memory scores may still demonstrate differences in immediate recall vs delayed recall. Hypothesis H4 addresses whether the reduction in redundancy and improvements in interpretation provide sufficient justification for accepting a loss of detail.

The basic method for determining how well the research results support the statistical hypotheses is through traditional statistical procedures. Each assessment compares the data with a null hypothesis H_0, representing a no-effect baseline. The p-value is the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming H_0 is true. Smaller p-values represent greater evidence of H_0 being incorrect. A predetermined level of α = 0.05 is used as the criterion for determining when to reject H_0. An additional aspect of this analysis includes creating confidence intervals (CIs). If you were to randomly sample multiple times from the same population using the same methods, 95% of those CIs would contain the true population parameter.

Bootstrapping generates new datasets using random sampling with replacement from your original dataset. These new datasets allow you to create a simulation of what your sampling distribution of a statistic might look like. From these bootstrapped datasets, you can determine the 2.5th percentile and 97.5th percentile of your distributions to create a bootstrap confidence interval. The z-score describes how many standard deviations away from the mean of a specific reference distribution a given score is. With the standardized scoring on the instruments used in this study, we are able to compare scores from different tests.

Cohen provided guidelines regarding the size of effects based upon the standardized difference (d): d = 0.20 represented a small effect, d = 0.50 was a medium effect, and d = 0.80 represented a large effect. In chi-square analyses, Cramér's V provides information about the strength of association. As such, I am utilizing descriptive standards to help interpret the magnitude of association; i.e., V = 0.10 represented a small effect, V = 0.30 represented a moderate effect, and V = 0.50 represented a large effect.

While it seems plausible to extract severity groups/strata from data, the level of distinctiveness of the strata is still unclear. Because the bootstrap resampled assessments rather than patients, repeated assessments may have increased apparent stability and reduced uncertainty around the estimates.

blocks.section: Hypothesis 2: Imputation Sensitivity Under a Fixed Partition
blocks.tested_text:
I have also tested Hypothesis 2. This hypothesis stated that when you use the same partial data set in an identically designed imputation environment, it can reasonably be expected that the results of clusterings based upon the data sets developed through an identically defined process, will show substantial similarities under a fixed embedding and partition. Using UMAP + HDBSCAN, I found all three primary tiers in my main analyses. To conduct my second level of sensitivity analysis, I performed a StandardScaler, then a UMAP, then a K-Means labeling rule with k=3 on the MICE-imputed domain scores. I did this on each of the other imputed data sets. Because I had already fit my models to the MICE-imputed domain scores, I could only vary the imputed values. Therefore, I matched up all possible methods so that I had 45 pairs of methods. My average ARI was .710 and my median ARI was .739. The lowest ARI value I obtained was .509 while the highest ARI value I obtained was .880. The mean consensus fraction was 0.929. There were at least eight out of ten methods that agreed on how they assigned members to their respective clusters in 86.2% of all assessments.

Therefore, as it relates to H2 and as stated, the assignments of members to clusters are relatively stable across many methods used to replace missing values within an identified single embedding and partitioning model. However, this does not confirm whether or not multiple independently fitted pipelines constructed via UMAP + HDBSCAN will identify similar hierarchical densities. The numbers of clusters generated for each complete-pipeline solution ranged from k=3 to k=5. The numbers of clusters produced in the five separate MICE complete-pipeline runs ranged from k=3 to k=7. This type of variability is consistent with treating a continuum as if it were discrete; however, it is not sufficient to prove this characterization.

blocks.tested_text:
Hypothesis 3 assesses if there are any associations between the cognitive-severity tier and clinical-unit assignment. A chi-square test demonstrated a statistically significant relationship between the two (χ^2 = 911.3, p ≈ 4 × 10^-156), with Cramér's V=0.162. This is a small effect under Cohen's descriptive guidelines, but exceeds the study's specified cutoff of 0.10. In addition, when calculating the mean Cramér's V over five independent MICE imputations, a similar average of 0.154 was calculated. Therefore, this represents a summary of sensitivity estimates across multiple imputations rather than an inference based on Rubin’s pooling rules.

A stratified sensitivity analysis also found that the association persisted even after controlling for the broad diagnostic grouping which is provided in the clinical-unit lookup. Since these diagnostic groupings were created using the same lookup data that provides the detailed unit assignments, this result should not be considered to represent any form of independent predictive validity.

Patient-grouped multinomial models gave no clear evidence that tier would improve classification of the detailed clinical units beyond the broad diagnostic grouping. Log loss for diagnosis alone was 0.6064, while log loss including tier was 0.6051, representing a decrease of 0.0013. Its 95% patient-bootstrap interval was [-0.0006,0.0031], which includes zero. The accuracy scores were 0.7772 and 0.7770, respectively, and macro-F1 scores were 0.476 and 0.480, respectively. As such, I consider H3 to be supported only insofar as it represents an association hypothesis, and does not establish added predictive value.

The hypothesis for this comparison was that by reducing redundancy, features of an aggregate domain will be easier to interpret than the separate individual variable approach, but they should maintain separation similar to the separate variable method. I examined cluster separation by comparing silhouette values and compared the quality of the feature spaces as represented by the condition numbers. To measure the amount of multicollinearity in each representation, I calculated the variance inflation factor (VIF).

Average silhouette improved with aggregating tests within domains; it went from 0.473 to 0.481 (see Figure 4.11). However, there was much larger improvement when examining the conditioning of the feature space. The average VIF dropped from 2.77 to 1.88, and the condition number dropped from 61.7 to 11.8. Large VIFs indicate high levels of multicollinearity among variables. As such, if there are correlated variables influencing distance calculations made by both UMAP and HDBSCAN then smaller VIFs would mean fewer redundant influences on the distances after data has been grouped into a cognitive domain. Additionally, groupings by cognitive domain allow for easier understanding and relating the results to the constructs measured by those tests [Lezak et al., 2012].

The main support for Hypothesis 4 comes from a reduction in redundancy and better numerical conditioning and interpretability. However, there is very little difference in the silhouette scores indicating no substantial improvements in clustering separation.

A random forest surrogate model was constructed based on the MICE-imputed domain scores using the pre-existing tier label values to define the target variable. Cross validation across five folds resulted in an overall accuracy rate of 99.4%, demonstrating that the boundary partitions derived from the same domain scores can be replicated. Although this demonstrates the reproducibility of partition boundaries, it does not independently establish natural cluster separation or predict clinical outcomes.

The Gini Importance ranking for these domains was: Orientation (0.486); Visuoperception (0.237); Language (0.171); Memory (0.061); Attention (0.028); and Executive Function (0.018). As seen in Figure 4.12, Permutation Importances provided similar ordering for the three top-ranked variables with attention ranked lowest. These results detail which variables reproduce the chosen tier labels. If multiple variables are highly correlated, there will likely be overlapping or substitutable effects among them when assessing their contribution, thus influencing both their ordered ranks [Boulesteix et al., 2012] and ultimately their relative importance to the prediction. Therefore, even if a predictor has a low surrogate importance value, it does not necessarily indicate that the predictor is clinically unimportant. Additional insights into the severity continuum are presented through the domain profile and principal component analysis in Section 4.4.

I did additional research to see how robust the hypothesis findings were. First, I generated a baseline using a list-wise deletion approach. Next, I did an additional test called a subsample-stability test. Then, I created Bootstrap Confidence Intervals. Afterward, I ran independent MICE imputations and compared the results to those I had found originally. Additionally, I entered into the model each individual's progression through their tier levels (i.e., each subject's transition in tier level over time) and the amount of time (in days) since the injury. Lastly, I applied an adjustment to each of the 45 pairwise H2 statistical tests to control for testing multiple times.

Bootstrap Confidence Intervals. Using assessment-level resampling, I calculated the average ARI (Adjusted Rand Index) for H2 to be .710; 95% CI [.702, .717] and Cramér's V for H3 to be .166; 95% CI [.156, .175]. For H4, the silhouette gap was -.002; 95% CI [-.021, .013]. The H4 confidence interval includes zero, so it appears there is no support for increased separation of individuals based upon this additional comparison. Since these are estimates that are derived separately from the initial findings and need not reflect the same results as the headline numbers, the initial raw-test aggregation used in the supplementary feature comparisons differ from the standardized patient-level process. In addition, because this resampling treats all 17,406 assessments as if they were independent (although they actually came from 7,285 different patients), the intervals may appear tighter than warranted; they do not capture any uncertainty due to resampling patients as units.

H2 and Multiple Comparison Correction. To compare all possible combinations (forty-five total) of cluster assignments using the specified cutoff (ARI > 0.50), I used Holm-Bonferroni adjustment to control family-wise Type I error and Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment to control the false discovery rate. Using one-sided parametric bootstrap p-values for each combination, the null-hypothesis was rejected for forty-four of the forty-five combinations at both family-wise and FDR corrected significance levels. KNN–SoftImpute was the borderline case; its ARI had a mean bootstrap value of 0.509 and 95% CI of [0.497, 0.521].

Across-Imputation Sensitivity Summary. To assess variability across imputations, I created M = 5 independently generated MICE imputed datasets and completed the full pipeline on each dataset. Across all nonlinear statistics, I present the cross-imputation mean (Q̅) as well as a descriptive dispersion interval for that statistic defined as Q̅± t_0.975,4√((1+1/M)B) , where B represents the sample variance of the five estimates. Since no estimation of the within-imputation variance exists, these intervals represent only the between-imputation variation and should be interpreted as such. Due to the non-linear nature of Cramér's V and silhouette, they do not represent Rubin-rule confidence intervals. Rather, they serve as sensitivity analyses providing summaries of how much the results can vary based upon different plausible sets of imputed data. The overall mean Cramér’s V was 0.154 with a descriptive interval of [0.049, 0.259]. The average silhouette gap was 0.050 [0.043, 0.058]. The number of recovered clusters ranged from three to seven. Domain-level features outperformed variable-level features in each of the five runs.

Following removal of 46.9% of the total number of assessments containing missing values, I then completed the remainder of the pipeline with the remaining 9,245 complete case assessments. This generated a two-cluster solution with a silhouette measure of .257. However, they are not identical. As such, the use of imputation does affect how one conducts their analysis; removing 46.9% of assessments may result in differing numbers or qualities of levels/tiers as defined by this study.

The median pairwise ARI was 0.277. Fifteen fits produced a solution that consisted of two clusters, while three fits found a solution consisting of three clusters. Two fits did not produce any type of clustering solution. As such, the historical UMAP + HDBSCAN tiering assignment has considerable sensitivity based upon resampling. Missingness Threshold Sensitivity. I repeated the full process of variable selection, domain computation, MICE imputation and UMAP + HDBSCAN clustering using five Tier-1 thresholds from 30% to 70%. As Figure 4.13 shows, at thresholds from 40% through 70%, the tier number ranged from two to three, while the silhouette scores ranged between 0.39 and 0.52. However, once a threshold of 30% was applied to the analysis, the restriction placed upon the variables resulted in a failure of the system. Therefore, the historical threshold sweep provided here will evaluate how sensitive the selected variables and resultant pipeline are and not whether the primary saved matrix was produced using a 50% row-missingness limit. The established row rule is described in Section 3.2.

Time Since Injury and Tier Transitions. The median time since injury for individuals in the Above-Average group is 214 days, 188 days for individuals in the Near-Normal group, and 172 days for those classified as Global Impairment. Due to their nature, cross-sectional comparisons do not allow for an assessment of an individual's overall level of recovery and should never be considered as an independent measure of functional status. Out of a total of 5,206 patients who had at least one repeat assessment, there were 2,613 (or roughly 50.2%) whose tier classification did not change during any of their observed visits, while there were 2,593 (roughly 49.8%) whose tier classifications changed. Among these patients, 912 had exactly two assessments and experienced a change in tier classification: 706 of whom moved to a higher-tiered classification and 206 of whom moved to a lower-tiered classification. This represents movement within cognitive-score bands but does not establish validated functional improvement. Factors such as timing of visit; discharge; and availability of tests may have affected observed tier transitions.

blocks.section: Cognitive Structure and the Limits of Phenotype Claims
blocks.tested_text: The historical assessment showed a broad cognitive-severity structure among individuals with acquired brain injury (ABI). Patient-level extensions showed consistent score groupings that varied based upon scale selection and imputation. These assessments, individually and collectively, did not provide evidence for distinct clinical phenotypes; conversely, there was no direct evidence suggesting that clinical phenotypes may be non-existent. To classify historical assessments in the "above-average", "near-normal", or "global-impairment" tiers, I looked at performance across the whole battery. While each tier has different levels of performance, each does not represent a unique shape of performance. All six areas of the assessments produced similar patterns of movement. As can be observed in Figure 4.5, the first principal component explained approximately 56% of the total variability in domain scores. Additionally, it loaded positively on every single one of the six areas at virtually equivalent magnitude. Based upon this information, I interpret the results as showing a pattern of severity-based stratification, as opposed to identifying specific cognitive patterns. Furthermore, the tiers were associated with clinical unit assignment (see §4.7), but this analysis did not show additional predictive value beyond the broader diagnostic grouping.

blocks.section: Cognitive Structure and the Limits of Phenotype Claims
blocks.tested_text: In addition to the findings demonstrating the extent to which variation in neuropsychological test performance reflects variation associated with the domain tested versus a general factor, the findings further illustrate the size of the proportion of the recoverable structure within this routine data collection cohort that is accounted for by a general severity dimension. While secondary variations related to domain specificity were observed, I found no evidence to indicate that they would be responsible for determining clusters. Therefore, based upon the findings of these analyses, there exists empirical support for both clinical experience (i.e., global impairment patterns as a method of separating patients prior to identifying dissociative patterns) [Maas et al., 2017], and the positive manifold of inter-test correlations commonly reported in neuropsychological studies [Lezak et al., 2012]. The results of the phenotypic analysis presented herein also indicate that the findings represent a somewhat conservative estimate of the phenomenon being studied when contrasted with those of previous examinations. For example, even after applying robustness procedures (i.e., imputation-based sensitivity testing) overall severity emerged as a defining characteristic of subgroups before profile pattern characteristics were identified. Given that domain-based aggregation and density-based clustering occurs along manifolds that are characterized by the presence of a general factor accounting for most of the variance among tests, I do not attach significant importance to the absence of evidence indicating narrow dissociations, including attention-specific subgroups, which may exist but be undetectable due to their small magnitude or orthogonal nature relative to the primary severity gradient.

blocks.section: Cognitive Structure and the Limits of Phenotype Claims
blocks.tested_text:
While this current research does not conflict with previous studies on the variety of dissociable cognitive profiles that arise from brain injury [García-Rudolph et al., 2021] in terms of whether or not such profiles do exist, the results provide a qualification of how these prior findings should be interpreted. The methodology used by García-Rudolph et al. differs from mine in several ways. First, the methodology I employed (UMAP + HDBSCAN) allows identification of irregular shapes and/or "noise" at low densities. Second, I used assessment resampling to assess cluster reproduction. Finally, I standardize, winsorize, and align all of my variable measures in a specific direction before creating composite variables. Each preprocessing decision is significant -- especially given large variance in raw score measurements (such as subject's completion time for Trail Making Tests), creation of artificial axes due to non-cognitive data, or large amounts of missing data where the density estimates may be skewed. Therefore apparent differences in phenotypes due to pre-processing decisions may not represent real structure differences in neuropsychology. This is discussed further in Chapter 6.

The first hypothesis was only partially supported (Section 4.5). All ten imputation methodologies produced adequate levels of both silhouette and noise metric assessments. In other words, all ten of the imputation methodologies recovered ordered bands of severity. However, while overall core Jaccard varied across the ten methodologies from 0.509 to 0.630, individual matched-cluster comparisons varied from 0.383 to 0.633 and cluster identifications were identified between three and five. These results support ordered severity bands, but do not establish sharply defined, uniformly reproducible phenotypes. Phenotype boundaries can shift without disrupting the underlying severity banding order.

Although I believe my method for dealing with the imputed data affected how many tiers I found, as well as their quality, I am inclined to think that my findings regarding the position of patients on the cognitive-severity continuum may vary less depending on what kind of imputation technique I employ. Overall, the fixed-reference diagnostic preserved many of the assignments between all compared imputations. The claim does not hold up when we examine independent model fits: the new KNN sensitivity yields an ARI of 0.538 against the reference three-group partition. That being said, while I do not feel these results indicate that missing data should be ignored, I would say that researchers can develop approaches to address missingness systematically and report on the methodology they use, and clinicians can treat tier labels as resources to support decision-making and judgment, rather than as replacements for educational, training and experiential based practice.

There was an obvious difference in the characteristics of both the smooth, model-based (EM, DAE, VAE) vs. the local/donor-type (KNN) imputation techniques (see Figure 4.9). While there is literature that categorizes various types of imputation methodologies (machine learning/statistical/deep learning), it seems to me that another way to categorize imputation methodologies is to separate them into two families: the "smooth" family of models where imputed values generally trend towards a model-based conditional mean, and local/donor models where estimates for a single assessment are made using a few neighboring assessments (donors).

A consensus cluster vote produced a value representing how much agreement existed regarding assignment of labels to individual assessments based upon the voting results of the different imputation strategies. Although MICE is generally accepted to replace missing data prior to clustering on neurocognitive test data, if a researcher anticipates that relationships between neuropsychological assessment variables will likely be nonlinear, MissForest [Stekhoven and Bühlmann, 2012] has been shown to perform well. Due to application of the Holm-Bonferroni adjustment procedure to each of the 45 pairs of comparisons (as described in Section 4.10), 44 of the 45 pairs rejected the null hypothesis stating that ARI ≤ .50. The exception was KNN–SoftImpute, whose ARI remained near the threshold. Therefore, within the fixed-reference H2 design, I concluded that there does not appear to be a single strategy for replacing missing data that drives patient placement on the severity dimension. The number of density-based tiers remains more sensitive when UMAP + HDBSCAN is refitted independently.

The amount of sensitivity possibly present in the treatment of missing data is illustrated in Section 4.10. Comparison of complete case data resulted in differences in the number of clusters identified, where silhouette = .257 whereas ARI = .625 when comparing MICE-derived solutions to the shared assessments derived through raw test aggregation. While the controlled comparisons in the extension demonstrated some degree of sensitivity related to the directional and scaled alignment, previous list-wise statistical analyses do not represent domain standardized analyses.

In order to assess if there is an association between cognitive-severity tier and which clinical unit each participant was assigned to, I used a contingency test on both tier and unit. There was a statistically significant association, with a small effect size according to Cohen’s descriptive standards. This association was still present after controlling for the broader diagnostic category that was also provided through the clinical-unit lookup using a stratified sensitivity analysis. Since the broader category and unit details were both retrieved via the same clinical-unit lookup function, I did not view these two sources as providing independent validation.

Although the association may have some clinical implications, it cannot be taken as evidence of predictive capability or causality. When conducting a patient-grouped multinomial sensitivity analysis, when tier was added to the broad diagnostic grouping, held-out log loss decreased from 0.6064 to 0.6051. However, in assessing the patient bootstrap improvement interval for tier, zero was included; and accuracy was identical to three decimal points. Therefore, H3 provides only support for differences in tier distribution among units. Assessing prospective routing or future outcomes requires separate predictors, patient-grouped validation and clinical outcomes collected for that purpose.

blocks.tested_text:
Many ways exist to describe cognitive characteristics. Two general approaches use variable-level characteristics and aggregated characteristics. Variable-level characteristics evaluate each individual test by itself. Aggregated characteristics are averages or sums of tests and are designed to represent a specific cognitive domain. In my research, I tested whether an aggregated characteristic of a cognitive domain would have lower multicollinearity than a variable level characteristic. Better conditioning was assessed through lower variance inflation factors (VIF) and a lower condition number.

The results from my data analysis supported H4. My findings did demonstrate lower levels of multicollinearity when using domain-aggregated characteristics instead of variable level characteristics. More specifically, while I found that there were minimal differences in cluster separation (the silhouette value increased only slightly from 0.473 to 0.481), the average VIF decreased from 2.77 to 1.88 and the condition number decreased from 61.7 to 11.8 (see Section 4.8). Thus, I believe H4 provides evidence that aggregating domain-test scores can reduce redundancy and create a more interpretable and well-conditioned way of representing assessment data. It should be noted however that this finding does not provide evidence of materially stronger cluster separation. This advantage is also consistent with the practical use of assessing scores on a per-domain basis rather than examining them individually [Lezak et al., 2012].

I wanted to point out that there is a crucial requirement when you are combining test variables at the level of individual variables — all transformations at the variable level need to occur before the final step of aggregation. The data needs to undergo transformation (winsorization), alignment based on direction, and scale (standardization) before values from each variable can be put together into a single measure of overall performance or a composite. If this order is violated (i.e., if we aggregate values from different variables before standardizing those values), our results will artificially depend upon which variable has the greatest range because of its initial scale.

For instance, if several memory tests were aggregated prior to standardizing them, the final composite is likely to reflect the performance on the test(s) with the largest range rather than whatever aspect of memory it was intended to measure. Similarly, if multiple tests with a high degree of similarity (correlation) enter an unstandardized composite, UMAP and HDBSCAN may utilize the same dimension of cognition to inflate the distance computations.

Aggregating features produces a single feature per domain but does not necessarily ensure that each domain receives equivalent weighting after additional scaling. Additionally, as demonstrated by the patient-level extension, robust scaling provides a larger weight to the tails of both language and orientation.

The results in §4.9 describe relationships among the cognitive domains and the classifications of the random forest surrogate model. Since the random forest surrogate model was 99.4% accurate in reproducing labels from the same domain scores used to create them, I believe that the ordering generated from the random forest surrogate primarily represents where the random forest surrogate model identified the boundaries of each partition generated during the fitting process rather than the causal reasons underlying each of the partitions. For example, since the random forest surrogate ranked orientation, visuoperceptual ability, and language as being higher than attention and executive function, I don't place much emphasis on the ordering. This is due to high correlations between many of the domains. Additionally, the Gini importance can be greatly influenced depending on whether you have multiple highly correlated predictors [Boulesteix et al., 2012].

I place more weight on the principal component analysis (PCA). The PCA indicated that only one principal component accounted for approximately 56 percent of the total variance in the domain scores. Each of the six domains had positive loadings that were all roughly equal in size. Therefore, I believe that this supports a general severity dimension rather than domain-specific dissociation or an attention specific pattern within this particular domain aggregated pipeline. The checks in §4.10 showed considerable assignment variability under assessment subsampling, and tier counts varied with variable-inclusion thresholds. The results demonstrate why researchers conducting data-driven research on phenotyping should explicitly document how their data was pre-processed and provide sensitivity analyses along with providing their original research findings.

I interpret this study’s finding as evidence supporting a three-tiered cognitive severity stratification model. However, I see a lot of limitations to using such a model. As I view it clinically, the most significant implication is conservative; they could provide some way of summarizing relative cognitive severity; but they cannot serve as independent clinical decision-making strategies. The medical education and knowledge of local service systems, as well as the professional experience of the clinician responsible for the referral to the rehabilitation services system, will continue to dictate how patients will be placed when they enter the rehabilitation services system. At this time, I do not believe that this research provides enough justification for direct clinical application (beyond carefully interpreting cognitive severity and openly dealing with missing data).

Historically, clinical practitioners have employed visual methods to examine distributions of patient scores in order to identify which patients represent “outliers” or “atypical” cases. Based upon what was found in this study, I also feel that there continues to be merit in employing algorithms to find clusters and visually examining the distribution of scores in order to identify outliers. Many of the assessments contained in the study had indistinct boundaries among separate groups. As such, I consider the middle tier of cognitive severity to be a part of a continuum with a boundary area cut out from it. Rather than falling into discrete categories of sharp separation, the majority of individuals appear to be distributed across a broad range of cognitive severity. As such, I believe that any future tools developed should focus on identifying assessments that either have difficulty clustering or are close to the boundary between two adjacent areas/clusters rather than attempting to assign each individual assessment a definitive phenotypic category.

In all twenty imputed datasets, two-group k-means clustering was identified as the most appropriate method to cluster the patients with a mean validation ARI of 0.959. Repeating the assignment of patients to groups is essentially a different issue than validating the accuracy of a phenotype. The equal-domain scaling produced substantial changes in patient assignments based upon their performance on the various tests included in the cognitive battery (ARI = 0.243 versus robust-scaling) and reduced assignment agreement across imputations. Regardless of how reliable a particular partition is, it may still be affected by either the geometric characteristics of the distribution of scores for the tests administered or other factors associated with how the tests were administered. One advantage of having a strong language-test contrast in one of the robust-space groups is its descriptive utility; however, a clinical interpretation would need to be evaluated under additional measurement and missingness models.

Likelihood results from these analyses also provide a further perspective on the comparisons. Although the restricted t mixtures were able to better fit the incomplete observations than did the selected Gaussian alternatives, as well as favoring eight components at the search boundary (as did the Gaussian models), neither family provided sufficient evidence to support the conclusion of a particular optimal number of patient types. Moreover, although there appeared to be some increase in the likelihood of trajectories with increasing numbers of classes, no multi-class solution could be identified that would satisfy the criteria for a minimal number of members in each class. Therefore, neither analysis can refute the possibility of the existence of very small subgroups.

These results address several issues associated with recently developed methodologies for dealing with incomplete data, ensembles, and longitudinal data [Tong and Tortora, 2025; Tomo et al., 2026; Julià et al., 2026], that employed many of the ideas presented in this study. Nevertheless, both the implementation and cohort differ from those in the referenced studies. Thus, this study supports the idea that reproducible cognitive score-based subgroupings exist when certain analytical conditions are met; however, this study does not provide support for clinically distinct phenotypes. It appears that a comparison using independent outcomes of continuous scores alone versus scores plus group membership, followed by external replication, would be required to determine whether identifying patients into pre-specified groups provides meaningful additional information.

Firstly, there is only one research site for this study; consequently, every piece of data collected in this study originated from a single rehabilitation unit. This may lead to selection bias which means that the ability to generalize these findings to other clinical populations cannot be confirmed. However, the tests are extensively studied and have international validity, while the six cognitive domains provide a common framework for describing post-injury cognition. Validation across multiple sites is required prior to considering this severity structure to represent ABI broadly instead of representing this specific rehabilitation unit.

Secondly, most historical analyses treated the 17,406 assessments as separate observations rather than grouping them within the 7,285 patients. While it is true that the repeated follow-up assessments of the same patient(s) will always be correlated by definition, neither the primary clustering method nor the assessment level bootstrap accounted for this correlation. Although utilizing each individual assessment allows for preserving the history of recovery status documented in the clinical records at each point in time, utilizing each individual assessment also can potentially create an overestimation of cluster stability along with creating narrower confidence intervals than what exists when assessments are grouped by patient. The patient-grouped multinomial sensitivity analysis directly assesses H3. The new extension adds additional techniques for both discovery and validation at the patient-level including patient subsampling and integrated random effects trajectory estimation. The new extension does not revise the previously calculated uncertainty intervals resulting from the historical assessment-level analysis.

blocks.tested_text: Thirdly, the recovered model's structure imposes restrictions on how we are able to analyze our findings. Although the available historical data suggest that there exists a wide spectrum of possible degrees of severity, the extension demonstrates that while it is possible to establish replicable partitions amongst multiple ways of representing the same data, such partitions remain highly dependent upon which representation was used. Furthermore, it is not possible using the methodologies discussed herein to establish a singular categorical structure. A majority of the cohort exists along a single dimension that represents overall cognitive degree of severity. The fact that PC1 accounted for approximately 56% of the total variance in the domain scores is evidence of this. The three tiers established through clustering represent a discretized version of this continuum. As such, the tiers should not be viewed as distinct, phenotypic entities with sharply defined boundaries. The actual number of tiers established will likely be influenced by two factors; namely, how one defines the threshold values separating the cluster(s) from one another and what proportion of the data is missing. Assessments that occur near the boundaries of each tier should also be approached with caution. A continuous severity score may be more representative than discrete tiers (Section 6.2).

Fourthly, the analytical methodologies have a limited ability to assess the temporal changes that occur post-injury. As previously mentioned, ABI recovery generally occurs very quickly in the initial phase and slowly thereafter [Ponsford et al., 2014; Maas et al., 2017]. Thus, a single evaluation represents a "snapshot" of an injured person's recovery process at a specific time. Many individuals had multiple evaluations in the dataset, allowing researchers to assess if they could detect patterns or trends of change; however, the timing of follow-up evaluations varied greatly as it depended on clinical needs rather than being part of a standardized protocol.

Of the total population of 5,206 patients who had longitudinal data available (Section 4.10), 50.2% remained in the same tier throughout all their study visits. The subset of 912 patients who had exactly two assessments and demonstrated a tier change showed a greater percentage of patients demonstrated increases in scores (n=706) compared to decreases (n=206); thus, the results are compatible with recovery, yet tier movement is not a functional outcome. There are additional variables that may impact tier movement including selection, discharge from care, timing of assessments, and availability of tests.

Further longitudinal studies with standardized assessment time frames are needed to address this question.

Another limitation is how missing values were imputed. As noted previously, it has been shown that the MAR assumption cannot be evaluated using only the observed data [Rubin, 1976; Little and Rubin, 2019]. For example, a patient may have a missing test score because he/she is unable to complete it. Therefore, if there is a Missing Not At Random (MNAR) mechanism for missingness, then the imputation of those missing values could overestimate test performance. Our comparisons do not provide an upper bound on this bias. We are planning to perform a formal sensitivity analysis of a "delta shift" to assess potential violations of our working assumptions regarding missingness.

Structured co-occurrence of missingness is consistent with test-battery protocols, but does not distinguish protocol-driven from outcome-dependent non-completion. Under a fixed MICE-fitted rule, at least 80% of the ten methods agreed on the assignment for 86.2% of assessments. This supports conditional assignment robustness, but does not establish ignorable missingness or agreement among independently fitted pipelines.

Assessment eligibility required at least one observed retained test, so records with many missing entries could be included. The higher number of required observations (seven tests) produced an index-patient population of 6,602. The adjusted Rand Index (ARI) value comparing these to the three-group assignments made by comparison on shared validation patients was 0.903. These results suggest some robustness in regards to excluding records based on sparseness; however, the status of the cognitive state of excluded encounters continues to remain uncertain.

The new observed-data mixture model addresses an issue with the previous historical method (impute-then-cluster) by integrating over missing coordinates. This new model continues to have assumptions about missing data (ignorable), utilizes continuous distributions as approximations for discrete and bounded score values, and uses a "dispersion-floor" to prevent singular solution(s). Fthe of the 32 attempts at fitting the models failed to meet the requested level of convergence. Both selected t-distribution families reached eight components, the upper end of the search. As such, the exact number of unique classes identified within these mixtures remain unknown. Additionally, I chose not to implement either skew-t or multivariate contaminated longitudinal models.

As such, feature engineering is still applicable. We remove all non-cognitive measures from the dataset. All test directions and scales are aligned. Winsorization is applied prior to creating composite scores through aggregation. Some potential artificial profile differences could arise based upon those decisions. Researchers will need to assess how variables were scaled, what variables were utilized in addition to how the study population was defined when assigning a clinical label to a distinct phenotype discovered using exploratory methods.

Four prospective areas of research are identified based on the results and constraints discussed earlier.

One implication of the cognitive-severity gradients is that continuous indices of cognitive-severity (e.g. produced through PCA, or produced using supervised learning methods on metrics related to functional performance) can potentially provide better representations of patient status and can be used as better summaries of patient status than categorical tiers. Future studies should investigate how well continuous cognitive-severity indices perform relative to tiered classification schemes in terms of predicting prognosis and determining the optimal intensity of rehabilitation required based upon the needs of the individual, while acknowledging that tiered classification may represent an meaningful discrete representation of continuous data as opposed to representing inherent categories.

A second area of expansion would involve developing the linear random-effects mixture model for repeated assessments taken at fixed intervals, thereby allowing investigators to understand longitudinal development of individuals' recovery trajectories. Specifically, the relationship between initial position along the cognitive-severity gradient at assessment and long term outcomes, as well as whether there are different rates of recovery associated with different levels of severity, could be investigated [Ponsford et al., 2014]. As previously mentioned, the selection of this longitudinal subset of trajectories was based on available visits and length of follow-up. Additionally, many other aspects remain unexamined including non-linear patterns of change, informative dropout, and additional externally derived measures of function. This current analysis has not established the value of these longitudinal subsets for either prognosis or rehabilitation planning.

blocks.section: Implications for Research and Clinical Interpretation
blocks.tested_text:
Continuous cognitive summaries and descriptive groups may remain candidates for future outcome validation. The current labeling system should include definitions used in preprocessing as well as any degree of uncertainty regarding those labels. These labels must not determine treatment intensities or routes for rehabilitation. Associations with clinical units or repeated cognitive assessments alone will not be sufficient to establish if treatments have produced clinically-relevant outcomes; however, CogDash presents both alternative designs for analyzing research and limitations for evaluating results and making comparisons among profiles from models that were saved during testing.

Empirical priorities for future research include: (1) comparing independently assessed outcome measurements based on continuous scores versus continuous scores with cluster membership; (2) examining the sensitivity of identified effects to missing data, especially where such data are informative; and (3) examining test-administration procedures. Furthermore, replicating the observed relationship among different sites at different time periods is also an empirical priority for future research. Nonlinear longitudinal modelling and the assessment of adequately measured small subgroups may serve as a foundation for future research that does not assume additional mixture components reflect legitimate patient types.

superseded_blocks.tested_text:
There are also correlations between test-availability and the fixed cluster allocations. Cramér's V on cluster vs. missingness was 0.412 for MRAVLT075 and 0.371 for FEPMR. Both tests exhibited substantial variation in missingness across clusters: 10.2 – 80.4 % for MRAVLT075 and 16.1–86.3% for FEPMR. While these appear to indicate a relationship among cluster allocation and missingness, they do not support the conclusion that missingness is causing the partitioning of data. Nevertheless, there is sufficient variability to disallow our treatment of the reliability estimates based upon only one of the imputation methods as representing the absence of test administration effects.

Mean imputation at k=3 yielded an ARI of 0.921 compared to the original groupings, whereas, K-nearest neighbors (KNN) at k=3 yielded an ARI of 0.538. Requiring at least seven observed tests retained 5,263 discovery and 1,339 validation patients, with ARI 0.903 on shared validation patients. Removing clipping gave ARI 0.958. With a fifty-iteration limit, deterministic imputation converged at iteration 37 and left labels unchanged (ARI = 1.000). Clustering validation subjects independently with the frozen discovery transformation produced an ARI of .895. This is a measure of agreement not a second performance metric predicated upon prediction.

Comparing raw-test aggregation against direction-aligned standardized domain results in ARI’s for the three groups of 0.703 for all assessments and 0.629 for complete-cases. The correlation between the two attention composite measures was -0.749 for construction, thus suggesting that the alignment of scales/directions affected these measures. These are descriptive sensitivities with completed values held fixed, not a replication of the earlier supplementary multiple-imputation and complete-case analyses.
